instruction:
Write exactly ONE sentence, about 12–16 words, and nothing after it.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

reply: That is good news, I was just hoping to pay three thousand dollars for moving.

blind_reason: The reply says it's good news and that they hoped to pay $3,000, which reads as mocking the company's "bargain" claim, so it means the opposite of its literal words.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

Reply to them with a short sarcastic remark (one or two sentences).

prompt:
Write exactly ONE sentence, about 12–16 words, and nothing after it.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

Rules for the ending:

- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

prompt:

- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:

- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

blind_reason: The reply says it's good news and that they hoped to watch 92 slides, but it clearly means the opposite, mocking the length of the presentation.

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

Someone says to you: "Our flower girl refused to walk down the aisle and sat on the floor."

Reply to them with a short sarcastic remark (one or two sentences).
reply: That is good news, I was just hoping to watch a child sit on the floor.
reason: The reply sarcastically claims to be pleased about the child sitting on the floor, which means the opposite of its literal words, and it directly fulfills the request for a sarcastic remark.
blind_reason: The reply claims it's "good news" and that the speaker hoped to see a child sit on the floor, which is clearly mocking and not meant literally.

Reply to them with a short sarcastic remark (one or two sentences).

prompt:
Write exactly ONE sentence, about 12–16 words, and nothing after it.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

blind_reason: The reply feigns pleasure at the vacuuming, saying the opposite of what any sympathetic listener would mean, which is clearly sarcastic.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

reply: That is good news, I was just hoping to miss the deadline by ten minutes.
reason: The reply feigns happiness that the deadline was missed, saying the opposite of what a real reaction would be, which is clearly sarcastic and fits the request.
blind_reason: The reply says it's good news and claims to have wanted a missed deadline, which is clearly the opposite of what's meant, so it reads as sarcasm.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

reply: That is good news, I was just hoping to watch ninety-two slides one by one.

blind_reason: The reply says it's good news and that they hoped to watch 92 slides, which clearly means the opposite given the context of a tedious presentation.

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

blind_reason: The speaker says "good news" and claims to hope to shovel wet snow, which is a chore people dislike, so the words mean the opposite of what they say and mock the excitement.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist.

Use this template: "That is good news, I was just hoping to [plain everyday activity]."

The activity must be the person's actual bad situation, or its direct, ordinary consequence, described in plain literal words, as if you wanted it. Examples:
- Deadline moved up: "That is good news, I was just hoping to work through the weekend."
- Bibliography trouble: "That is good news, I was just hoping to spend hours fixing citations."
- Noisy neighbours: "That is good news, I was just hoping to hear drilling all afternoon."

Rules for the ending:
- Use common, boring words, the way you would describe a normal day.
- Do NOT invent a scenario, prop, or contrast image (no costumes, choirs, coats, "experience," "skills," or "adventure").
- Do NOT exaggerate or make it absurd or clever. Plain and literal is the point; the "good news… hoping to" framing supplies the irony.
- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

Avoid intensifiers and stock markers: no "truly," "really," "I'm sure," "fantastic," "wonderful," "exactly," "of course," "at least," and no exclamation marks. Use only one ironic idea.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist.

blind_reason: The reply says it's "good news" and that she hoped to be treated like a project, but it means the opposite, mocking the guy's insulting question.

- End with one simple, ordinary noun or time phrase, then a period.

The reply must still be clearly sarcastic. The ending must name something unpleasant from their situation, so it is obvious you mean the opposite of "good news." Never just praise or restate their words without the "hoping to" twist. Respond directly to what the person said, in a dry, flat tone.
